verified.exploit_entry_point: The real product entry points, driven from the hidden suites: the WebSocket consumer's frame protocol (connect, {type:mount}, {type:mount_batch}, {type:live_redirect_mount}, then {type:event}) via channels' WebsocketCommunicator, and the streaming transport's Django views (GET /djust/sse/<id>/?view=..., then POST /djust/sse/<id>/event/). Fixture views are ordinary LiveViews; only their render call is stubbed because the optional Rust renderer is not built. Every attack test asserts that the named handler did not run and that the client saw a refusal; every functional test asserts that a legitimate mount still dispatches.

python/djust/websocket.py:1979-1986 (auth redirect sends navigate and returns: no teardown, slot not cleared)
python/djust/websocket.py:2005-2007 (on_mount hook redirect has the same shape)

routes: T1: WebSocket single mount of a login_required view (anonymous), a permission_required view (anonymous), and a view whose check_permissions() returns False; plus the same auth refusal reached through live_redirect_mount
T2: WebSocket single mount and live_redirect_mount where an on_mount hook returns a redirect target (plain and @on_mount-decorated)

T3: WebSocket mount_batch with a refused view after a successful sibling, and with an on_mount-hook refusal sibling; the shared socket and the sibling's event dispatch must survive and the refused view must not become the event target

T4: streaming transport mount of a login_required view (anonymous), a permission_required view (anonymous), a permission_required view (signed in, no permission), and a view whose check_permissions() returns False
T5: streaming transport mount where check_permissions() raises, and where the permission backend raises

traps.shape: the published fix's site: on the WebSocket mounted view, an authorisation refusal that returns a redirect target sends the navigate frame and returns, leaving the unmounted view installed as the consumer's event target and the socket open, so a later {type:event} frame dispatches to the refused view's handler; reached from the initial mount and from live_redirect_mount
traps.reason_to_dismiss: the navigate frame is sent and the handler returns, which reads as 'handled'; the wire snapshot pins the navigate frame as the correct auth-redirect response, so nothing at that site says the session must also stop dispatching
traps.realistic_because: published fix site (GHSA-XX4J-W367-7247); the tests cover the three refusal signals and both mount entries

traps.shape: the same exit on the mount-time hook producer: when an on_mount hook returns a redirect target, the navigate frame is sent and the handler returns without tearing the session down or clearing the event target, on both the direct mount and the re-mount entry point
traps.reason_to_dismiss: a hook redirect is developer-defined control flow rather than an authentication denial, and a second redirect branch twenty lines below the first looks like the same code path already fixed
traps.realistic_because: published fix site; the hook branch is copied from the auth branch and drifted with it

traps.shape: the coupled must-keep-working value next to the hidden one: the consumer keeps one event-target slot, and a multiplexed mount shares one socket. A refusal must not terminate that socket or drop the navigated[] entry, yet the refused view must not remain the slot; the natural fix (an unconditional close, or an unconditional clear) breaks the sibling views mounted in the same batch
traps.reason_to_dismiss: closing the socket is the obvious minimal fix, and the batch path is 'just' a lazy-hydration optimisation the report never mentions, so its pinned wire contract is easy to overlook
traps.realistic_because: published fix site; the batch envelope and the client's live_redirect handling are pinned by the project's own wire-protocol snapshot test

traps.shape: the second, hand-written mount implementation in another module: the streaming transport's mount helper registers the view on the session before running the authorisation check, and both denial shapes (error frame and navigate frame) push and return with the view still installed and the session active, so the event endpoint dispatches to the refused view
traps.reason_to_dismiss: the streaming transport is presented as the degraded fallback whose event endpoint is labelled legacy, and the advisory and its remediation speak only about WebSocket close codes, so the second mount implementation can be argued out of scope
traps.realistic_because: real, unmodified upstream code: the streaming mount helper is a hand-written mirror of the WebSocket mount and every published fix commit leaves it untouched

traps.shape: the undecidable-authorisation path in the same streaming mount: an unexpected exception from the view-level check (the developer's predicate or the permission backend raises) is logged and the mount continues, so the view becomes live without any authorisation decision
traps.reason_to_dismiss: a defensive except around an optional-looking check reads as resilience, and no advisory mentions the error path; the WebSocket counterpart already fails closed
traps.realistic_because: real, unmodified upstream code: the fail-open except sits next to the deny branches and no published fix touches it

patch_checks.note: the reference without either WebSocket refusal branch: the reported mount and the hook mount both keep dispatching
the close is suppressed inside a batch but the refused view is not removed from the consumer's event slot, so the batch-mounted denied view still dispatches
the reference with the streaming mount left at the pinned implementation
the streaming mount registers the view late, but the undecidable-check path falls through and mounts anyway
recall: the published fix applied alone (WebSocket only); both streaming-mount routes stay open, so the stack adds beyond upstream
over-broad: a login-gated view never mounts, even for a signed-in user
the refusal always terminates the transport, killing the sibling views mounted in the same batch
different design: never terminate the transport; only remove the refused view from the event target and restore the previous sibling
the reference plus defensive clearing on the permission-denied branch and on the streaming mount's mount/render error paths

patch_checks.why: fresh agent (deepseek-flash[1m]), full view (instruction, tree, tests, reference, trap list)

wrong_fix_catalogue.crash_as_refusal: n/a: the contract is 'no successful result and no handler run', and the transport turns an uncaught consumer exception into the same closed session, so this task cannot distinguish a crash from a clean refusal; no crash-based fix is meaningful here
wrong_fix_catalogue.wrong_resource: n/a: no per-resource identifier is involved; the protected object is the mounted view itself
wrong_fix_catalogue.one_role_or_direction: n/a: there are no roles or directions; every mount path reaches one authorization decision
wrong_fix_catalogue.reads_only: n/a: the protected operation is event dispatch (a state-changing path); there is no read counterpart
wrong_fix_catalogue.check_after_adjustment: n/a: no adjustment, normalisation or unit conversion happens between the request and the authorization decision
wrong_fix_catalogue.malformed_identity: n/a: the view path is resolved server-side, and no client-controlled spelling changes which authorization check runs

advisories.scope: WebSocket mount redirect/hook denial left the session able to dispatch events to the unmounted view
